docs.title: RLT for Python
docs.text:
Fit random forests for continuous responses, class labels, and right-censored survival times with a scikit-learn-style interface. rlt brings the tree algorithms of the RLT R package to Python.

For installation, examples, and the R interface, see the R version documentation.

The default forest uses one variable at each split. Optional reinforcement uses embedded forests to guide variable selection. Linear-combination splits split along a direction formed from several predictors and can be used with or without reinforcement.

Get started: install and fit a forest

docs.title: Install from source
docs.text: These guides describe the GitHub source version, 0.3.0. Install it from the source repository, using the installation instructions for shared Python dependencies and system libraries. The standard build targets Linux; Windows and macOS need additional compiler and linker configuration.

docs.title: Predict a continuous response
docs.text:
After installation, fit on 160 simulated observations and predict the 40 held out before fitting. The response depends on the first two predictors plus noise.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_reg

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 6))
y = X[:, 0] - X[:, 1] + rng.normal(size=200)

model = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=100, mtry=3, nsplit=0,
    resample_replace=True, resample_prob=0.8,
    random_state=1, n_jobs=1,
).fit(X[:160], y[:160])
pred = model.predict(X[160:])

print(f"OOB MSE: {model.oob_error_:.3f}")
print(f"Test MSE: {np.mean((pred - y[160:]) ** 2):.3f}")

OOB MSE: 1.401
Test MSE: 1.847

Both numbers are mean squared prediction errors; smaller is better. Each out-of-bag (OOB) prediction uses only trees that omitted that training row. Test MSE evaluates the separate 40-row test set. Their difference here is one small-sample result, not evidence that one evaluation method is generally better. The first-analysis walkthrough also shows individual predictions and explains the fitting controls.

docs.title: Choose your analysis
docs.text: Task Start here Main result Predict a continuous response Regression Predicted response means and OOB/test MSE Predict a class Classification Class labels and probabilities in classes_ order Model a censored event time Survival Conditional survival curves, cumulative hazards, and OOB concordance error

docs.title: Understand and inspect a fitted forest
docs.text:
• Variable importance: measure the change in OOB predictive loss when a variable is perturbed.
  • Linear combinations: allow up to several predictors in a split direction.
  • Survival confidence bands: construct nominal simultaneous bands separately for each target curve over its returned time grid.
  • Forest kernels: inspect which observations share terminal nodes, with separate ordinary, training, and OOB calculations.
  • Individual trees: read named splits and terminal predictions with tree_summary().
  • Model workflows: work with labeled data, inspect OOB availability, request prediction uncertainty, and save fitted models.

See reproducibility to control simulation and forest randomness, or comparing Python and R for numerical agreement, source matching, and interface differences.

docs.title: Citations and license
docs.text:
Cite the papers for the methods used in your analysis:

  • Reinforcement learning trees: Zhu, R., Zeng, D., and Kosorok, M. R. (2015). Reinforcement Learning Trees. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 110(512), 1770-1784.
  • Matched-sample variance estimation: Xu, T., Zhu, R., and Shao, X. (2024). On variance estimation of random forests with Infinite-order U-statistics. Electronic Journal of Statistics, 18(1), 2135-2207.
  • Survival confidence bands: Formentini, S. E., Liang, W., and Zhu, R. (2022). Confidence Band Estimation for Survival Random Forests. arXiv preprint, arXiv:2204.12038.

The survival paper develops the cumulative-hazard covariance and Gaussian simulation framework for the bands. See the get_surv_band reference for the current smoothing and covariance handling.

RLT for Python is distributed under GPL (>= 3), inherited from the R package.

docs.title: Survival Confidence Band
docs.text:
This page demonstrates how to construct simultaneous confidence bands for conditional survival curves at chosen predictor values. The example uses the smoothed covariance approach in get_surv_band() and simulated data whose true curves are known.

The cumulative-hazard covariance and Gaussian simulation framework for these bands is developed in Formentini, Liang, and Zhu (2022). The get_surv_band reference describes the current smoothing and covariance handling.

Two details matter for interpretation:

  • Check that target predictor values are represented in the training data, especially for the important variables, to limit extrapolation.
  • Inspect how many observations remain at risk over time. The far tail has less support when few observations remain under follow-up without an event.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
We simulate right-censored survival data from a proportional hazards model. The first and third predictors carry signal; the rest are noise.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_surv

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

n = 200
p = 10
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))

def xlink(x):
    return np.exp(x[:, 0] + x[:, 2] / 2)

FT = rng.exponential(1.0 / xlink(X))
CT = np.minimum(6, rng.exponential(1.0 / 0.25, size=n))

time = np.minimum(FT, CT)
event = (FT <= CT).astype(bool)

y = np.empty(n, dtype=[("event", "?"), ("time", "<f8")])
y["event"] = event
y["time"] = time

docs.title: Target Points
docs.text:
We choose two target points at interior quantiles of the important variables X1 and X3. The remaining variables are fixed at their training medians.

target_base = np.median(X, axis=0)
testX = np.tile(target_base, (2, 1))

testX[:, 0] = np.quantile(X[:, 0], [0.35, 0.65])
testX[:, 2] = np.quantile(X[:, 2], [0.35, 0.65])

np.round(testX[:, [0, 2]], 3)

array([[-0.384, -0.385],
       [ 0.315,  0.377]])

docs.title: Fit and Predict with Variance
docs.text:
We use var_mode="matched" to estimate covariance of the predicted cumulative hazard over time, which is the scale used by the band calculation. The 1,000 trees form 500 matched pairs using half-samples without replacement. Matched mode enforces these sampling settings and reduces an odd requested tree count to the preceding even count; at least two trees are required. The settings are explicit below.

For the matched-sample variance framework, see Xu, Zhu, and Shao (2024).

fit = RLT_surv(
    n_estimators=1000, mtry=min(p, 10), min_samples_leaf=5,
    nsplit=3,
    resample_prob=0.5, resample_replace=False,
    importance="none", verbose=0,
    n_jobs=1,
    var_mode="matched",
    split_rule="logrank",
    random_state=2,
)
fit.fit(X, y)

prediction = fit.predict_details(testX, var_est=True)
S, cov = prediction["Survival"], prediction["Cov"]
S_reference = np.exp(-prediction["CHF"])

docs.title: Choose a Display Range
docs.text:
The fitted model can return predictions over the observed event-time grid, but the far right tail has little data support. For this example, we only display the region t <= 2. This cutoff is an illustration, not a criterion establishing sufficient support. The band is constructed over the full returned grid, even when the plot shows only part of it.

risk_set = np.array([np.sum(time >= t) for t in prediction["timepoints"]])
plot_time_max = 2
plot_id = prediction["timepoints"] <= plot_time_max

if not plot_id.any():
    plot_id = np.zeros_like(plot_id, dtype=bool)
    plot_id[0] = True

print(f"Plot time range: t <= {plot_time_max}")
print(f"Minimum at-risk in plotted range: {int(risk_set[plot_id].min())}")
print(f"Number of plotted timepoints: {int(plot_id.sum())}")

Plot time range: t <= 2
Minimum at-risk in plotted range: 33
Number of plotted timepoints: 136

docs.title: Simultaneous Confidence Band
docs.text:
With alpha=0.05, get_surv_band() constructs a nominal 95% simultaneous band separately for each target's conditional survival curve over the returned grid. It does not provide joint coverage across targets, continuous-time coverage between grid points, or a prediction interval for a target's event time.

The reference curve is S_reference = np.exp(-prediction["CHF"]). It equals S for this ordinary forest. For a linear combination forest, returned survival is instead the mean of tree product-limit curves, whose variation is not directly estimated by this CHF-based band.

The smoothed approach uses a low-rank covariance approximation and a residual correction to form marginal standardizing scales. Here k_rank=10 allows up to ten components in that approximation. Gaussian simulations retain the original supplied CHF covariance; nsim controls the number used to estimate the simultaneous critical value. See get_surv_band for smoothing and numerical implementation details.

from rlt import get_surv_band

SurvBand = get_surv_band(prediction, alpha=0.05, approach="smoothed",
                         k_rank=10, nsim=5000, seed=0)

The saved result already contains CHF, its covariance, and the selected time vector. Reusing it for another rank or confidence level avoids recomputing forest predictions. The model convenience call get_surv_band(fit, testX, ...) remains available. A tracking-only fit can use var_mode="IJ" or "jack" in that call, or in predict_details, when the fitted resampling counts support the requested method. The plot below retains the raw reference curve and band arrays; only the displayed probability axis is restricted to [0, 1].

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharey=True)
titles = ["Interior lower-risk target", "Interior higher-risk target"]

for i, ax in enumerate(axes):
    tp = prediction["timepoints"][plot_id]
    S_i = S_reference[i, plot_id]
    truth = np.exp(-xlink(testX)[i] * tp)

    b_lower = SurvBand["lower"][i, plot_id]
    b_upper = SurvBand["upper"][i, plot_id]

    ax.fill_between(tp, b_lower, b_upper, color="#3b82f6", alpha=0.25,
                    label="Simultaneous 95% Band")
    ax.plot(tp, truth, color="#E41A1C", lw=2, ls="--", label="True S(t)")
    ax.step(tp, S_i, where="post", color="black", lw=2, label="Estimated S(t)")

    ax.set_title(titles[i])
    ax.set_xlabel("Time")
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)

axes[0].set_ylabel("Survival Probability")
axes[1].legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Select a figure to view it at full size.

The higher-risk target has larger values of both signal variables, so its true survival curve falls faster. In this realization, that true curve falls outside the band at some displayed times. A nominal 95% simultaneous band need not contain the true curve in every dataset, and one realization cannot establish coverage. Each band was constructed on the full returned grid, although only the portion through time 2 is displayed.

docs.title: Optional Rank Selection
docs.text:
The smoothed approach can also choose the rank by cumulative eigenvalue proportion instead of a fixed k_rank:

SurvBand_prop = get_surv_band(
    prediction, alpha=0.05,
    approach="smoothed",
    k_mode="proportion",
    k_prop=0.95,
)

Increasing nsim improves Monte Carlo precision for the simulated critical value at the cost of runtime. Python and R use different random streams, so the same integer seed does not imply identical simulated band limits. Smoother diagnostics report its GCV parameters and convergence; parameters can be unstable when the GCV objective is flat even if the fitted surface is stable. Numerical agreement between implementations does not establish the method's statistical coverage.

docs.title: Random Forest Kernel
docs.text:
forest_kernel() measures similarity by counting how often observations share a terminal node in the fitted forest. The ordinary self-kernel and cross-kernel return integer counts across all trees. Dividing by fit.params_.ntrees gives leaf-sharing frequencies in [0, 1], not weights that sum to one across a row.

With vs_train=True, each shared-leaf contribution is multiplied by the training observation's in-bag multiplicity for that tree. Bootstrap repeats can therefore produce counts larger than the number of trees. This mode requires retained sampling counts, enabled by resample_track=True or an active var_mode at fitting. Supply the original training X as X2, in its original row order. The API checks the row count, but cannot detect shuffled or replaced rows. The OOB self-kernel in Example 3 uses a different, pair-specific normalization.

docs.title: Example 1 - Axis-aligned
docs.text:
We build a regression forest using "best" splits and compare ordinary leaf-sharing counts with in-bag-weighted counts.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_reg

# ---- Generate a small dataset (about 100 obs) ----
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 120
p = 5
X = rng.uniform(size=(n, p))
y = X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] + rng.normal(size=n)

# Train the forest (axis-aligned "best" splits)
fit_rect = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=300, mtry=p, min_samples_leaf=5,
    nsplit=0,  # "best" splits: consider all cut points
    resample_prob=0.8, resample_replace=True,
    importance="permute",
    resample_track=True,
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit_rect.fit(X, y)

# Choose a target point
newX = np.full((1, p), 0.5)
newX[0, 1] = 0.3

# Leaf-sharing counts between newX and all X
KW_rect = fit_rect.forest_kernel(newX, X)

# Map counts to marker areas for display only.
size_scale = 180 * KW_rect[0] / KW_rect[0].max()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8))

# X0 vs X1 (both are signal features)
axes[0, 0].scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], s=8, color="deepskyblue")
axes[0, 0].scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], s=size_scale, color="darkorange",
                   alpha=0.6, linewidths=0.5, edgecolors="black")
axes[0, 0].scatter(newX[0, 0], newX[0, 1], marker="x", s=100,
                   color="black", linewidths=3)
axes[0, 0].set_title("Rectangular kernel - X1 vs X2")

# X0 vs X2 (X3 is noise)
axes[0, 1].scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 2], s=8, color="deepskyblue")
axes[0, 1].scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 2], s=size_scale, color="darkorange",
                   alpha=0.6, linewidths=0.5, edgecolors="black")
axes[0, 1].scatter(newX[0, 0], newX[0, 2], marker="x", s=100,
                   color="black", linewidths=3)
axes[0, 1].set_title("Rectangular kernel - X1 vs X3")

# Use the original training rows, in their original order.
KW_rect_train = fit_rect.forest_kernel(newX, X, vs_train=True)
size_scale_train = 180 * KW_rect_train[0] / KW_rect_train[0].max()

axes[1, 0].scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], s=8, color="deepskyblue")
axes[1, 0].scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], s=size_scale_train, color="darkorange",
                   alpha=0.6, linewidths=0.5, edgecolors="black")
axes[1, 0].scatter(newX[0, 0], newX[0, 1], marker="x", s=100,
                   color="black", linewidths=3)
axes[1, 0].set_title("In-bag-weighted counts - X1 vs X2")

# Another projection
axes[1, 1].scatter(X[:, 1], X[:, 2], s=8, color="deepskyblue")
axes[1, 1].scatter(X[:, 1], X[:, 2], s=size_scale, color="darkorange",
                   alpha=0.6, linewidths=0.5, edgecolors="black")
axes[1, 1].scatter(newX[0, 1], newX[0, 2], marker="x", s=100,
                   color="black", linewidths=3)
axes[1, 1].set_title("Rectangular kernel - X2 vs X3")

for ax, (xlabel, ylabel) in zip(
    axes.flat, [("X1", "X2"), ("X1", "X3"), ("X1", "X2"), ("X2", "X3")]
):
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Select a figure to view it at full size.

Orange marker area is proportional to the count, scaled separately for each kernel; the black cross marks the target. This display scaling does not turn counts into probability weights, and marker areas cannot be compared between the ordinary and in-bag-weighted plots. The projections show how similarity varies along the signal variables (X1, X2) and the noise variable (X3).

docs.title: Example 2 - Linear-combination
docs.text:
We use SIR loadings to split on combinations of up to two predictors and plot the resulting leaf-sharing counts. See Linear Combinations for direction estimation and the embedded-model reference for predictor screening.

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 120
p = 3
X = rng.uniform(size=(n, p))
y = X[:, 0] + X[:, 2] + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=n)

fit_lc = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=300, mtry=p, min_samples_leaf=5,
    nsplit=3,
    resample_prob=0.9, resample_replace=False,
    linear_comb=2,
    linear_comb_method="sir",
    importance="permute",
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit_lc.fit(X, y)

newX = np.full((1, p), 0.5)
newX[0, 1] = 0.3
KW_lc = fit_lc.forest_kernel(newX, X)
size_scale_lc = 180 * KW_lc[0] / KW_lc[0].max()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
ax.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 2], s=8, color="deepskyblue")
ax.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 2], s=size_scale_lc, color="darkorange",
           alpha=0.6, linewidths=0.5, edgecolors="black")
ax.scatter(newX[0, 0], newX[0, 2], marker="x", s=100, color="black",
           linewidths=3)
ax.set_title("Linear-combination kernel - X1 vs X3")
ax.set_xlabel("X1")
ax.set_ylabel("X3")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The larger orange markers lie along a descending band in the two signal variables. Points in this band have similar values of X1 + X3, illustrating how combination splits can make leaf sharing follow a signal direction.

docs.title: Example 3 - OOB self-kernel
docs.text:
The OOB self-kernel compares training observations using only trees where both observations are out-of-bag. Each contributing tree was fitted without either observation in the pair. It requires retained sampling counts, enabled by resample_track=True or an active var_mode at fitting, and the original training data as X1, in the original row order. As with vs_train=True, the API checks the number of rows but does not verify their identity or order.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_reg

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, p = 120, 5
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
y = X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] + rng.normal(size=n)

fit = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=300, nsplit=2,
    resample_track=True,  # retain sampling counts for the OOB kernel
    n_jobs=1, random_state=1,
)
fit.fit(X, y)

out = fit.forest_kernel(X, oob=True)
K, N, C = out["Kernel"], out["N"], out["C"]
# K = C / N where N > 0, and 0 otherwise

N[i, j] counts trees where observations i and j are both out-of-bag; C[i, j] counts those trees where they also land in the same terminal node; Kernel = C / N normalizes them into [0, 1]. Pairs that are never OOB together (N = 0) get Kernel = 0.

print(K.shape)    # (120, 120)
print(N[0, 1], C[0, 1])   # 48 1
print(np.trace(K))        # 120.0; diagonal is 1 wherever N > 0

Use N to distinguish an unsupported pair (N = 0) from an observed zero leaf-sharing count. These matrices describe the fitted forest; using them in a degrees-of-freedom estimator requires that estimator's own assumptions.

docs.title: Random Seed and Reproducibility
docs.text: This page explains how to control randomness in your analyses with rlt's random_state, the Python counterpart of RLT's seed argument. Data simulation has a separate NumPy seed.

docs.title: Where to set the seed
docs.text:
With rlt, randomness lives in two places: your data simulation (numpy) and the forest's internal resampling (random_state on the estimator).

  • For fully reproducible data + model, seed your numpy Generator at the top of the script and pass a fixed random_state to each estimator.
  • If your data are fixed and only modeling randomness matters, only the estimator's random_state needs to be fixed.

Prerequisites: See Get Started.

docs.title: Demonstration: same forest seed, same results
docs.text:
We simulate one dataset and fit it twice with the same forest seed. This holds the training data and test data fixed while checking the forest's randomness.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_reg

# Shared forest configuration
ntrees = 200
nmin = 5
mtry = 5
samplereplace = True
sampleprob = 0.80
nsplit = 0

# Simulate once, independently of the forest seed.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
trainn = 80
testn = 20
n = trainn + testn
p = 10
X1 = rng.normal(size=(n, p // 2))
X2 = (rng.uniform(size=(n, p // 2)) * 3).astype(int)  # integers 0,1,2
X = np.hstack([X1, X2])
y = (
    1
    + X[:, 1:6].sum(axis=1)
    + 2 * np.isin(X[:, p // 2], [1, 2])
    + rng.normal(size=n)
)
trainX, trainY = X[:trainn], y[:trainn]
testX, testY = X[trainn:], y[trainn:]

def run_forest(seed):
    """Fit the fixed training data, changing only the forest seed."""
    fit = RLT_reg(
        n_estimators=ntrees,
        mtry=mtry,
        min_samples_leaf=nmin,
        resample_prob=sampleprob,
        resample_replace=samplereplace,
        nsplit=nsplit,
        importance="permute",
        categorical_features=range(p // 2, p),
        n_jobs=1,
        random_state=seed,
    )
    fit.fit(trainX, trainY)
    pred = fit.predict(testX)

    return (
        float(np.mean((fit.oob_prediction_ - trainY) ** 2)),
        float(np.mean((pred - testY) ** 2)),
        pred,
    )

# ---------- Run A (seed = 1) ----------
mse_oob_A, mse_test_A, pred_A = run_forest(1)

# ---------- Run B (same seed = 1) ----------
mse_oob_B, mse_test_B, pred_B = run_forest(1)

# ---------- Summary for same-seed runs ----------
print(f"A OOB MSE:  {mse_oob_A:.6f}")
print(f"A test MSE:  {mse_test_A:.6f}")
print(f"B OOB MSE:  {mse_oob_B:.6f}")
print(f"B test MSE:  {mse_test_B:.6f}")
print(f"Same-seed predictions identical: {np.array_equal(pred_A, pred_B)}")

A OOB MSE:  2.416684
A test MSE:  4.664737
B OOB MSE:  2.416684
B test MSE:  4.664737
Same-seed predictions identical: True

docs.title: Demonstration: change only the forest seed
docs.text:
Now we fit the same training data with a different forest seed and evaluate on the same test data. Differences therefore reflect forest randomization, rather than a new simulated dataset.

# ---------- Run C (seed = 2) ----------
mse_oob_C, mse_test_C, pred_C = run_forest(2)

print(f"C OOB MSE:  {mse_oob_C:.6f}")
print(f"C test MSE:  {mse_test_C:.6f}")
print(f"Diff-seed predictions equal to Run A: {np.array_equal(pred_C, pred_A)}")

C OOB MSE:  2.473170
C test MSE:  4.857821
Diff-seed predictions equal to Run A: False

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Choose an integer seed and record it with the data and model settings.
  • Keep one seeded np.random.default_rng(...) near the top of your script to make the whole workflow reproducible.
  • The same pattern works for classification and survival: place the data-simulation seed before model fitting and give each estimator a fixed random_state.
  • random_state also accepts a NumPy RandomState or Generator instance; a fresh seed is drawn from it for each forest. Use a separate generator for data simulation.
  • When random_state=None, fitting draws from NumPy's global RNG, so np.random.seed(...) controls omitted forest seeds. This does not make NumPy's surrounding random stream match R's.

docs.title: Cross-language note
docs.text: In this Python port, random_state maps directly to the C++ master seed (the same argument R's RLT() calls seed), and numpy handles your data simulation separately. For cross-language comparisons, supply the same data, forest seed, and explicit parameter values. Matching a surrounding set.seed(...) call to a NumPy data-generation seed does not produce the same data. Numerical libraries and source revisions can also affect results; cross-platform bitwise identity is not promised.

docs.title: Single Tree
docs.text: This page shows how to inspect a single tree grown inside an rlt forest using get_one_tree(). For a readable table, use print_tree(0) or retrieve its columns with tree_summary(0).

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
We generate continuous and categorical predictors with a continuous outcome.

import numpy as np

# (Optional) For reproducibility in this tutorial only.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

# ---- Generate a small synthetic dataset ----
trainn = 80
testn = 20
n = trainn + testn
p = 10

# Continuous + categorical predictors (last half as categorical)
X1 = rng.normal(size=(n, p // 2))
X2 = (rng.uniform(size=(n, p // 2)) * 3).astype(int)  # integers 0, 1, 2
X = np.hstack([X1, X2])

# Continuous outcome with a simple signal + noise
y = (
    1
    + X[:, 1:6].sum(axis=1)
    + 2 * np.isin(X[:, p // 2], [1, 2])
    + rng.normal(size=n)
)

# Train / test split
trainX, trainY = X[:trainn], y[:trainn]
testX, testY = X[trainn:], y[trainn:]

docs.title: Fit
docs.text:
from rlt import RLT_reg

ntrees = 200
nmin = 5
mtry = p // 2
samplereplace = True
sampleprob = 0.80
rule = "best"
nsplit = 0 if rule == "best" else 3
importance = "permute"

fit = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=ntrees,
    mtry=mtry,
    min_samples_leaf=nmin,
    resample_prob=sampleprob,
    resample_replace=samplereplace,
    nsplit=nsplit,
    importance=importance,
    categorical_features=range(p // 2, p),
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit.fit(trainX, trainY)

docs.title: Inspect one tree
docs.text:
Use get_one_tree(tree_id) to inspect a single tree. Choose tree_id from 0 to fit.params_.ntrees - 1 (0-indexed, unlike R's 1-based indexing). Here we take the first tree:

tree = fit.get_one_tree(0)
tree.keys()

dict_keys(['SplitVar', 'SplitValue', 'LeftNode', 'RightNode', 'NodeWeight', 'NodeAve'])

The arrays are independent copies aligned by node index. Classification also returns NodeProb; survival returns the nested NodeHaz arrays; linear-combination trees include SplitLoad. Editing an extracted tree does not change predictions from the fitted model.

Array Meaning SplitVar Variable index split at this node; -1 for terminal nodes SplitValue Numerical threshold or encoded categorical partition; use tree_summary to decode it LeftNode / RightNode Child node indices NodeWeight In-bag count without sample_weight; normalized observation-weight mass otherwise, including resampling repeats NodeAve Terminal-node response mean; internal-node entries are placeholders

When sample_weight is supplied, fitting normalizes these weights to sum to one across the training data. NodeWeight sums that normalized mass over the in-bag copies reaching the node; it is not an observation count. This example is unweighted, so the summary's n column contains counts.

n_nodes = len(tree["SplitVar"])
n_splits = int((tree["SplitVar"] >= 0).sum())
print(f"{n_nodes} nodes, {n_splits} internal splits")

35 nodes, 17 internal splits

A compact preview from the public summary shows numerical thresholds and categorical right partitions:

def print_tree_preview(summary, max_lines=14):
    for i in summary["Node"][:max_lines]:
        split, value = summary["Split"][i], summary["Value"][i]
        if split == "leaf":
            detail = f"leaf | mean = {float(summary['Prediction'][i]):.3f}"
        elif isinstance(value, list):
            detail = split + " {" + ", ".join(map(str, value)) + "}"
        else:
            detail = f"{split} <= {value:.3f}"
        print(f"node {i:>3} | n = {int(summary['n'][i]):>4} | {detail}")
    if len(summary["Node"]) > max_lines:
        print("\n... output truncated ...")

For linear-combination forests, the loadings of every internal split live in fit.forest_["SplitLoad"][tree_id], aligned with the SplitVar rows. Each row has linear_comb coefficient slots, but a split can use fewer predictors; unused slots are zero. Categorical splits use a single predictor.

fit_lc = RLT_reg(n_estimators=50, mtry=3, nsplit=3,
                 linear_comb=3, linear_comb_method="sir",
                 categorical_features=range(p // 2, p),
                 n_jobs=1, random_state=1)
fit_lc.fit(trainX, trainY)

loadings = np.asarray(fit_lc.forest_["SplitLoad"][0])
loadings.shape  # (n_nodes, linear_comb)

np.round(loadings[0], 3)  # coefficients of the first split

docs.title: RLT with Linear Combinations
docs.text:
Linear-combination splits allow each internal node to split on a weighted combination of several variables rather than a single predictor. This can help when the signal is carried by a direction such as X1 + X2 instead of one coordinate at a time.

The example below uses regression. The same idea can also be applied to classification and survival forests by using RLT_cla or RLT_surv and choosing a model-appropriate linear_comb_method.

docs.title: Regression Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

n = 160
p = 6
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))

y = 1 + X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] + 0.5 * X[:, 2] + rng.normal(size=n, scale=0.5)

train_id = np.arange(120)
trainX, trainY = X[:120], y[:120]
testX, testY = X[120:], y[120:]

Fit a regression forest that considers linear combinations of up to three variables at a split. Here linear_comb_method="sir" selects sliced inverse regression (SIR), which uses the response to estimate a predictor direction. The tree then searches for a cutpoint along that direction. With nsplit=3, it compares three random candidate cutpoints; nsplit=0 would search all available cutpoints.

from rlt import RLT_reg

fit_lc = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=200,
    min_samples_leaf=5,
    mtry=3,
    nsplit=3,
    linear_comb=3,
    linear_comb_method="sir",
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=3,
)
fit_lc.fit(trainX, trainY)

print(fit_lc)

RLT_reg(linear_comb=3, linear_comb_method='sir', mtry=3, n_estimators=200,
        n_jobs=1, nsplit=3, random_state=3)

Linear combinations do not require reinforcement. This fit uses the default reinforcement=False.

docs.title: Prediction
docs.text:
test_pred = fit_lc.predict(testX)

print(f"Test MSE: {np.mean((test_pred - testY) ** 2):.4f}")
print(f"Maximum combination size: {fit_lc.linear_comb}")

Test MSE: 0.2817
Maximum combination size: 3

The held-out mean squared error summarizes prediction error on the 40 observations excluded from fitting. It describes this simulated dataset and fit. The stored combination setting confirms the maximum of three variables, not the number used at every split.

docs.title: Method names and integer codes
docs.text:
linear_comb_method also accepts the integer method codes used by the R package's core, which is useful when translating R code or tuning over methods programmatically. The names and codes are equivalent:

Model Names Codes RLT_reg naive, lm, pca, sir 1, 2, 3, 4 RLT_cla lda, naive, random, logistic 1, 2, 3, 4 RLT_surv coxph, naive 1, 2 
fit_code = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=200,
    min_samples_leaf=5,
    mtry=3,
    nsplit=3,
    linear_comb=3,
    linear_comb_method=4,  # integer code for "sir"
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=3,
)
fit_code.fit(trainX, trainY)

# identical forest to linear_comb_method="sir"
np.array_equal(fit_code.predict(testX), fit_lc.predict(testX))  # True

Like R, an unrecognized method name (or an out-of-range integer) does not error: it emits a UserWarning and resets to code 1, which is naive for regression, lda for classification, coxph for survival:

fit_bad = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=200,
    mtry=3,
    nsplit=3,
    linear_comb=3,
    linear_comb_method="ridge",  # not a valid method name
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=3,
)
fit_bad.fit(trainX, trainY)
# UserWarning: linear_comb_method not recognized. Use 'naive', 'lm',
#              'pca', or 'sir'. Resetting to naive

fit_bad.params_.linear_comb_method  # 1

docs.title: Other Model Types
docs.text:
For classification, use RLT_cla with methods such as "lda", "naive", "random", or "logistic".

For survival, use RLT_surv with methods such as "coxph" or "naive".

docs.title: Reuse predictions and inspect a fitted model
docs.text:
Use predict_details when you need predictions together with class labels, uncertainty, or individual trees. The usual predict, predict_proba, and two-item predict_var methods remain available.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_cla

rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
X = rng.normal(size=(80, 4))
y = np.where(X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0, "positive", "negative")
model = RLT_cla(n_estimators=60, resample_track=True,
                random_state=12, n_jobs=1).fit(X, y)

result = model.predict_details(X[:3], var_est=True, var_mode="ij", keep_all=True)
assert np.array_equal(result["Prediction"], model.predict(X[:3]))
assert result["PredictionAll"].shape == (3, 60, 2)
assert np.array_equal(result["classes"], model.classes_)

The last axis of PredictionAll follows classes; its entries are class probabilities. Regression returns an (n, trees) array. Survival returns AllHazard with shape (n, trees, times), together with timepoints. predict_all_trees provides these arrays directly for all three estimators. Negative regression or class-probability variance estimates are reported as NaN, as in R.

docs.title: Check which rows have OOB predictions
docs.text:
Some training rows have no out-of-bag predictions. Use the availability mask before summarizing OOB accuracy or interpreting labels.

oob = model.oob_details()
available = oob["available"]
oob_accuracy = np.mean(oob["Prediction"][available] == y[available])
assert oob["counts"].shape == (80,)

Unavailable class labels are None, and unavailable numeric outputs are NaN. The helper raises an error when OOB computation was disabled during fitting. The older oob_* arrays remain available, but their placeholder values should not be interpreted without the mask.

docs.title: Save a model and use it again
docs.text:
Pickle and joblib preserve the forest, effective parameters, category dictionaries, class order, survival grid, and retained sampling counts. Load model files only from sources you trust. Keep the package version and numerical environment with a saved model for reproducibility.

import pickle

saved = pickle.dumps(model)
restored = pickle.loads(saved)
assert np.array_equal(restored.predict(X[:3]), model.predict(X[:3]))

For a file, use joblib.dump(model, path) and joblib.load(path). Saving does not advance a supplied NumPy random generator. sklearn.base.clone continues to return an unfitted estimator with the requested constructor parameters.

docs.title: Keep labels when fitting data frames
docs.text:
Pandas is optional. Unordered categorical columns use categorical splits. For string labels that denote nominal groups, use an unordered pd.Categorical so splits can separate subsets of levels. Plain string columns instead use numerical ranks in sorted label order, which can impose an arbitrary ordering on nominal groups. Use an ordered categorical when its declared order is meaningful. Prediction reuses the training dictionary and matches named columns, so changing their order does not change their meaning.

import pandas as pd

frame = pd.DataFrame({
    "group": pd.Categorical(np.where(X[:, 0] > 0, "high", "low"),
                            categories=["low", "high", "unused"], ordered=False),
    "score": X[:, 1],
})
labels = pd.Categorical(y, categories=["positive", "negative"])
labeled = RLT_cla(n_estimators=40, random_state=12, n_jobs=1).fit(frame, labels)
assert labeled.classes_.tolist() == ["positive", "negative"]
reordered = frame[["score", "group"]].copy()
reordered["group"] = reordered["group"].cat.reorder_categories(
    ["unused", "high", "low"])
assert np.array_equal(labeled.predict(frame), labeled.predict(reordered))

Declared response levels determine probability-column order and tie breaking, including unused levels. Ordinary label arrays retain sorted observed class order. Unknown predictor labels and missing values are rejected. Plain numeric arrays can still use zero-based categorical codes with categorical_features.

For a fitted labeled predictor, a plain numeric prediction column means zero-based training codes. Keep a pandas categorical dtype when supplying numeric labels such as 10, 2 and 1, so they are matched as labels rather than mistaken for codes.

docs.title: Supply sampling counts
docs.text:
Pass resample_preset to fit to use a matrix of shape (rows, trees). Positive integers are in-bag multiplicities, zero means OOB, and negative integers exclude a row from both groups. Each column needs positive total mass no greater than the number of training rows.

from rlt import RLT_reg

preset = np.zeros((80, 4), dtype=int)
for tree in range(4):
    preset[tree:tree + 40, tree] = 1
preset[79, :] = -1
custom = RLT_reg(n_estimators=4, random_state=12, n_jobs=1).fit(
    X, X[:, 0] + X[:, 1], resample_preset=preset)
assert np.array_equal(custom.obstrack_, preset)
assert not custom.oob_details()["available"][79]

Matched, IJ, and jackknife fit modes replace a supplied preset with their sampling scheme and warn. As in R, prediction-time IJ/jackknife calculations on an ordinary tracked fit treat negative counts as zero. Their treatment therefore differs from fitting and OOB-kernel exclusion. Also, nominal full-sample settings can disable OOB predictions and importance even if a preset contains zeros.

docs.title: Inspect a tree or compute concordance
docs.text:
tree_summary(0) returns node depth, named splits, thresholds or category partitions, node weights, and terminal predictions. print_tree(0) displays the same information. get_one_tree(0) returns independent copies of all raw arrays, including class probabilities, survival node hazards, and linear-combination loadings. Tree indices start at zero.

tree = model.tree_summary(0)
assert tree["Depth"][0] == 0
assert "NodeProb" in model.get_one_tree(0)

from rlt import cindex
assert cindex([1, 2, 3], [1, 1, 1], [3, 2, 1]) == 1.0

For cindex(time, event, risk), higher risk means earlier failure. Times must be finite and events must be exactly zero or one. No comparable pairs or nonfinite risk scores produce NaN.

Concordance follows RLT's tie rules: equal risks receive half credit for distinct comparable times. Two events at the same time receive full credit for equal risks and half credit otherwise. At an event/censoring time tie, the observed event is treated as earlier; two censored ties are omitted.

docs.title: Variable Importance (Permutation and Distributed)
docs.text: Variable importance (VI) measures how much a fitted forest relies on each predictor for prediction. This page illustrates permutation and distributed importance using out-of-bag (OOB) observations, which were excluded from fitting the tree in which they are evaluated.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
We generate numeric and categorical predictors with a continuous outcome. The simulated response depends on predictors at indices 1 through 5. Each forest declares the last five columns in categorical_features. The figures label the ten predictors V1 through V10, corresponding to indices 0 through 9.

import numpy as np

# (Optional) For reproducibility in this tutorial only.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

# ---- Generate a small synthetic dataset ----
trainn = 80
testn = 20
n = trainn + testn
p = 10

# Continuous + categorical predictors (last half as categorical)
X1 = rng.normal(size=(n, p // 2))
X2 = (rng.uniform(size=(n, p // 2)) * 3).astype(int)  # integers 0, 1, 2
X = np.hstack([X1, X2])

# Continuous outcome with a simple signal + noise
y = (
    1
    + X[:, 1:6].sum(axis=1)
    + 2 * np.isin(X[:, p // 2], [1, 2])
    + rng.normal(size=n)
)

# Train / test split
trainX, trainY = X[:trainn], y[:trainn]
testX, testY = X[trainn:], y[trainn:]

docs.title: Option A - Permutation Importance
docs.text:
Set importance="permute" to measure the increase in OOB mean squared error after permuting a predictor. For each tree, the ordinary loss is the mean squared error on its OOB observations. The perturbed loss uses the same observations after shuffling the assessed predictor among them. The forest's importance is the average of these per-tree loss differences.

from rlt import RLT_reg

# Common fitting and resampling settings for both illustrations
ntrees = 200
nmin = 5
mtry = p // 2
samplereplace = True
sampleprob = 0.80
nsplit = 0

fit_perm = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=ntrees,
    mtry=mtry,
    min_samples_leaf=nmin,
    resample_prob=sampleprob,
    resample_replace=samplereplace,
    nsplit=nsplit,
    importance="permute",  # permutation-based VI
    categorical_features=range(p // 2, p),
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit_perm.fit(trainX, trainY)

# VI vector lives in feature_importances_
np.round(fit_perm.feature_importances_, 3)

array([ 7.500e-02,  5.440e-01,  1.290e-01,  5.340e-01,  2.100e-02,
        3.994e+00, -5.400e-02,  3.000e-03, -1.600e-02,  4.100e-02])

Here nsplit=0 searches all available cutpoints. Each tree draws 80% of the sample size with replacement, so an observation can be drawn more than once. OOB importance does not require retaining the resampling records with resample_track=True.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Simple visualization
predictor_names = [f"V{j + 1}" for j in range(p)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
ax.bar(predictor_names, fit_perm.feature_importances_)
ax.set_title("Permutation Variable Importance (rlt)")
ax.set_ylabel("Increase in OOB MSE")
ax.set_xlabel("Predictors")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Select a figure to view it at full size.

V6 has the largest permutation importance in this fit. A value near zero indicates little measured loss from permutation; a negative value means that permutation reduced the measured OOB loss. Such values can arise from sampling and forest randomness and do not prove that a predictor has no effect. Importance describes predictive reliance rather than a causal effect.

docs.title: Option B - Distributed Assignment Importance
docs.text:
Set importance="distribute" to route an OOB observation to both children at splits involving the assessed predictor, with probabilities proportional to the child node weights. Other splits follow the observation's predictor values as usual.

For a fixed tree and OOB observation with response \(y_i\), let \(q_{i\ell}\) be the resulting probability of reaching terminal node \(\ell\), whose prediction is \(\mu_\ell\). The distributed loss for that observation is

\[ \sum_\ell q_{i\ell}(y_i-\mu_\ell)^2. \]

The tree averages this expected squared loss over its OOB observations and subtracts its ordinary OOB mean squared error. The forest then averages the per-tree differences. The expectation is over squared losses along the routes; the method does not first average terminal-node predictions and then compute a squared loss.

The next fit uses the same data and fitting and resampling settings, changing only the importance method. Both methods need OOB observations; sampling almost all observations without replacement can leave too few for importance calculation.

fit_dist = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=ntrees,
    mtry=mtry,
    min_samples_leaf=nmin,
    nsplit=nsplit,
    resample_prob=sampleprob,
    resample_replace=samplereplace,
    importance="distribute",  # distributed assignment VI
    categorical_features=range(p // 2, p),
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit_dist.fit(trainX, trainY)

# VI vector lives in feature_importances_
np.round(fit_dist.feature_importances_, 3)

array([-0.005,  0.6  ,  0.116,  0.665, -0.018,  4.077, -0.065, -0.045,
       -0.023,  0.006])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
ax.bar(predictor_names, fit_dist.feature_importances_)
ax.set_title("Distributed Variable Importance (rlt)")
ax.set_ylabel("Increase in OOB expected squared loss")
ax.set_xlabel("Predictors")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

V6 also has the largest distributed importance in this fit. Both methods describe predictive reliance, but they perturb predictor use differently. Their rankings illustrate these two fits; common settings do not make the measures equivalent or establish a performance comparison. Near-zero distributed importance indicates little measured increase in loss; a negative value means the distributed expected loss was below the ordinary OOB loss. Neither proves that a predictor has no effect.

docs.title: Variance of variable importance (matched forests)
docs.text:
Fitting with var_mode="matched" and either importance option also estimates the variance of each VI estimate. These estimates help assess uncertainty in the fitted importance values.

The matched-sample variance framework is described by Xu, Zhu, and Shao (2024).

fit_vi = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=ntrees,
    mtry=mtry,
    min_samples_leaf=nmin,
    importance="distribute",
    var_mode="matched",   # per-variable variance of VI
    categorical_features=range(p // 2, p),
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit_vi.fit(trainX, trainY)

# (p,) variance of each VI estimate
np.round(fit_vi.var_vi_, 4)

array([ 5.00e-04,  1.07e-02,  1.39e-02,  3.79e-02, -2.72e-02,  5.44e-01,
       -5.50e-03,  3.80e-03, -1.00e-04,  1.33e-02])

importance_table() prints Variable and VI. When matched variance is available, the column named SD is the estimated standard error of the VI estimate, computed as SD = sqrt(VarVI). The table also reports the standardized statistic Z = VI / SD and a significance code (*** for \(|Z|\ge 2.58\), ** for \(|Z|\ge 1.96\), and * for \(|Z|\ge 1.64\)). These codes summarize the standardized values; they do not certify variable selection or causal importance. The layout mirrors R's print.importance.RLT:

fit_vi.importance_table()

Variable             VI           SD          Z  Sig
----------------------------------------------------------
V1              -0.0209     0.021899      -0.95
V2               0.5996     0.103274       5.81  ***
V3               0.0609     0.117999       0.52
V4               0.5832     0.194568       3.00  ***
V5              -0.0230           NA         NA
V6               3.8730     0.737591       5.25  ***
V7              -0.0231           NA         NA
V8              -0.0973     0.061325      -1.59
V9              -0.0141           NA         NA
V10             -0.0504     0.115454      -0.44

Note: 3 variable(s) with negative variance estimate (SD, Z shown as NA)

Two things to note in this output:

  • Negative variance estimates. The matched U-statistic variance can come out negative in a finite forest. Exactly like R, such variables get NA for SD and Z and an empty significance code, and the table appends a trailing Note counting them. A negative variance estimate does not by itself show that a variable is noise.
  • Without matched variance, the table simply has no SD / Z / Sig columns. importance_table() works for any importance != "none" fit and prints just Variable and VI.

The same table is available through the module-level function rlt.importance(model), mirroring R's importance(fit) idiom (the estimator attribute .importance holds the constructor parameter string, so the method could not take that name):

import rlt

rlt.importance(fit_vi)   # same table as fit_vi.importance_table()

Note

var_mode="matched" implies the matched-forest preset: subsampling without replacement at 50% and an even tree count. When importance is omitted, distributed importance is enabled automatically. Both importance="permute" and importance="distribute" can be requested explicitly; the selected importance measure is retained.

docs.title: get_surv_band
docs.text:
Nominal simultaneous bands for the conditional survival curve at each query point, using a saved survival prediction or a fitted RLT_surv. Coverage is specified separately for each curve over the returned time grid, without joint coverage across targets or coverage between grid points. These are not prediction intervals for an individual's event time.

The reference curve is exp(-CHF), and the covariance is on the CHF scale. For linear combination forests, the returned survival estimate is the mean of tree product-limit curves; this band does not directly estimate uncertainty in that different estimator.

For the matched-sample cumulative-hazard covariance and Gaussian simulation framework for survival bands, cite Formentini, Liang, and Zhu (2022), Confidence Band Estimation for Survival Random Forests. The current smoothing and covariance handling are described under Approaches.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_surv, get_surv_band

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 200
X = rng.normal(size=(n, 5))
t_event = rng.exponential(1 / np.exp(X[:, 0]))
t_censor = rng.uniform(0, 3, size=n)
y = np.empty(n, dtype=[("event", "?"), ("time", float)])
y["event"] = t_event <= t_censor
y["time"] = np.minimum(t_event, t_censor)

model = RLT_surv(n_estimators=1000, var_mode="matched",
                 resample_prob=0.5, resample_replace=False, random_state=42)
model.fit(X, y)

X_query = X[:3]  # training rows illustrate the API, not validation
prediction = model.predict_details(X_query, var_est=True)
reference = np.exp(-prediction["CHF"])
band = get_surv_band(prediction, i=0, alpha=0.05, approach="smoothed")
band["lower"], band["upper"]  # (n, T) band limits

docs.title: Signature
docs.text:
get_surv_band(
    model,          # saved prediction dictionary or fitted RLT_surv
    X=None,         # query covariates when supplying a model
    i=0,            # subject index: 0 = all, 1-based like R when positive
    alpha=0.05,     # level or array of levels
    approach="naive",
    nsim=5000,      # MC simulations for the critical value
    k_rank=10,      # rank truncation (smoothed approach)
    k_mode="fixed", # "fixed" or "proportion"
    k_prop=0.99,    # cumulative eigenvalue proportion (k_mode="proportion")
    seed=0,         # RNG seed for the MC band (deterministic given seed)
    band_grid_size=0,  # optional reduced time grid (see predict_var)
    var_mode=None,  # compatible override when supplying a model
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type / values Default Description model dict or fitted RLT_surv required Saved result with CHF, Cov, and timepoints, or a model supporting the requested covariance. X array-like (n, p) None Query covariates when supplying a model; omit with a saved prediction. i int 0 Subject selector: 0 = all subjects, k (1-based, like R) = subject k only. alpha float or array 0.05 Significance level(s); each must be in [0, 0.5]. approach "naive", "smoothed" "naive" Band construction; see below. nsim int 5000 Monte Carlo simulations for the critical value. k_rank int 10 Rank of the low-rank covariance truncation (smoothed). k_mode "fixed", "proportion" "fixed" Choose rank directly or by cumulative eigenvalue proportion. k_prop float 0.99 Target cumulative eigenvalue proportion when k_mode="proportion". seed int 0 Seed for the Monte Carlo critical value. band_grid_size int 0 Select a reduced grid during model prediction (0 = full grid). Saved results use their stored grid. var_mode None, "matched", "IJ", "jack" None Prediction-time override for a model. Matched requires a matched fit; IJ/jack require retained resampling counts. Saved covariance cannot be overridden.

docs.title: Approaches
docs.text:
• "naive": marginal SDs sqrt(diag(Cov)); Monte Carlo band with the full covariance matrix.
  • "smoothed": natural cubic regression spline tensor smoothing of the covariance surface, rank-k PSD truncation, positive-spectrum residual correction, and eigenvalue-ratio weights. The narrow Gaussian smoother follows R's mgcv 1.9-4 gam(z ~ te(i, j, k)) calculation on grid indices, including two curvature penalties, GCV selection, and the magic Newton/descent search. It runs through NumPy and SciPy without requiring R. Relabeling the time coordinates preserves the marginal scales. Grids with fewer than three times use the naive calculation with a warning.

This replaces the earlier Python actual-time B-spline approximation. Smoothed band values can change when upgrading. Frozen R fixtures check the basis, penalties, fitted covariance, and final scales across small grids, ranks, covariance scales, and singular cases. Near a GCV minimum, floating-point rounding can change the final parameter selection and its convergence flag. Tests measure this sensitivity against R itself and retain stricter checks with fixed smoothing parameters. For flat GCV objectives, smoothing parameters and EDF are not uniquely determined by the fitted surface.

Both methods simulate from the supplied CHF covariance. Smoothing changes the marginal standardizing scales. nsim controls Monte Carlo precision of the critical value; increasing it does not establish coverage. Monte Carlo draws use Python's seeded stream and need not match R for the same integer seed. Covariances must be positive semidefinite; only negative eigenvalues within R/Armadillo's scale-relative roundoff tolerance are clipped.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
A dict with:

Key Shape Description lower / upper (n_selected, T) or (n_selected, n_alpha, T) Limits for one or multiple alpha levels, respectively. timepoints (T,) The time grid used. diagnostics list of dicts Per-subject SDs, variance-explained, rank/eigenvalue info. marsd (n_selected, T) Final marginal standardizing scales. alpha (n_alpha,) Requested noncoverage levels. subjects (n_selected,) Selected 1-based subject numbers in the prediction.

Smoothed diagnostics include the selected smoothing parameters, EDF, GCV score, numerical rank, iterations, and convergence flag under diagnostics[j]["smoother"]. A flat or non-improving GCV search should be assessed alongside the fitted scales; its smoothing parameters alone do not measure uncertainty.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_surv, get_surv_band

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 200
X = rng.normal(size=(n, 5))
t_event = rng.exponential(1 / np.exp(X[:, 0]))
t_censor = rng.uniform(0, 3, size=n)
y = np.empty(n, dtype=[("event", "?"), ("time", float)])
y["event"] = t_event <= t_censor
y["time"] = np.minimum(t_event, t_censor)

model = RLT_surv(n_estimators=1000, var_mode="matched",
                 resample_prob=0.5, resample_replace=False, random_state=0)
model.fit(X, y)

# Naive band for the first subject
X_query = X[:3]  # illustration using training rows
prediction = model.predict_details(X_query, var_est=True)
band_naive = get_surv_band(prediction, i=1, alpha=0.05,
                           approach="naive", nsim=5000)

# Smoothed band with rank chosen by eigenvalue proportion
prediction_reduced = model.predict_details(X_query, var_est=True,
                                            band_grid_size=20)
band_smooth = get_surv_band(prediction_reduced, i=0, alpha=[0.05, 0.10],
                            approach="smoothed", nsim=5000,
                            k_mode="proportion", k_prop=0.95)

# A tracking-only fit can request IJ covariance at prediction time.
tracked = RLT_surv(n_estimators=1000, resample_track=True, random_state=0)
tracked.fit(X, y)
band_ij = get_surv_band(tracked, X_query, var_mode="IJ",
                        band_grid_size=20, nsim=1000)

A saved dictionary uses arrays with exact axes: CHF is (n, T), Cov is (n, T, T), and timepoints is (T,). The helper validates their dimensions and finite values, preserves the stored time vector, and does not modify the input arrays or recompute forest predictions. Select the grid and covariance mode before caching the result.

The returned limits are raw calculations and can extend beyond the probability range. Keep these arrays when inspecting results; use an axis limit such as plt.ylim(0, 1) for display. Restricting the plotted range does not change the time grid used to construct the band.

docs.title: Comparing Python and R results
docs.text:
The Python package shares RLT's tree algorithms and adds a scikit-learn interface. The current native source was synchronized with the corrected RLT 6.1.1 source tree. It includes the fixes for IJ count moments, weighted fitting, OOB kernels, and survival prediction grids.

For a numerical comparison, use the same input data, column order, explicit forest parameters, and integer forest seed. Python's random_state corresponds to RLT(seed=...). Seeding the surrounding NumPy and R data generators does not produce the same simulated data. Source revisions and numerical libraries also matter; a shared package version number alone does not establish an exact source match.

The tests compare fitted predictions and tracking records with an installed R package, and use small saved-tree fixtures to check variance and survival calculations directly. They check numerical behavior, not statistical coverage or a general predictive advantage.

docs.title: Interface differences
docs.text:
Python R Separate RLT_reg, RLT_cla, and RLT_surv estimators RLT(..., model=...) n_estimators=None resolves to 500 ordinarily or 100 with reinforcement 500 ordinarily; 100 when reinforcement is explicitly enabled Optional pandas categorical, ordered, and string columns; zero-based numeric category codes also supported Factor, ordered-factor, character columns, or numerical training codes Regression predictions have shape (n,); class predictions use the original labels Regression predictions have shape n x 1; class predictions are factors Survival covariance has shape (n, T, T) CHF covariance has shape T x T x n Separate predict_var method, which requires a supported uncertainty setup predict(..., var.est=TRUE)

predict_details provides complete public predictions, including class order, per-tree arrays, the exact survival grid, and uncertainty mode. Models support pickle/joblib, signed sampling presets, and labeled OOB inspection with explicit availability. See model workflows.

Python deliberately rejects fractional sampling counts and noncanonical primary boolean options instead of silently converting them. It also rejects missing or infinite concordance times. Declared categorical response levels retain their order; ordinary label arrays use sorted observed labels. Character sorting can depend on R's locale, so use explicit category levels for comparisons involving arbitrary text.

Both implementations preserve the full failure-time grid while fitting. Prediction on a reduced grid selects from complete cumulative-hazard curves. Ordinary survival forests return exp(-CHF); linear combination forests average the tree product-limit survival curves. Covariance remains on the CHF scale; confidence bands use exp(-CHF) as their survival reference in both cases.

docs.title: Smoothed confidence bands
docs.text:
Python's approach="smoothed" follows the narrow Gaussian mgcv 1.9-4 calculation used by RLT: natural cubic regression spline tensor margins on grid indices, integrated-curvature penalties, two GCV-selected smoothing parameters, and the magic Newton/descent search. It runs without R. Frozen R fixtures compare the design, penalties, fixed and optimized fits, and final marginal scales across grid sizes, ranks, covariance scales, and singular cases. This replaces the earlier Python actual-time B-spline approximation.

This is algorithmic alignment with the pinned smoother, with numerical tolerances for floating-point libraries. It does not imply bit-identical outputs across all BLAS/LAPACK versions or unique smoothing parameters when GCV is flat. Exact binary input and one-ULP perturbation controls show that R's final automatic selection and convergence flag can change near a numerical GCV minimum. Tests use that measured reference sensitivity for those cases, retain stricter fixed-parameter checks, and include a frozen independent holdout corpus. Diagnostics include the selected parameters, EDF, and convergence information. Different Gaussian random streams also mean that equal integer seeds need not produce equal Monte Carlo band limits.

Both approaches use the supplied CHF covariance for Gaussian simulation; smoothing changes marginal standardizing scales. Bands have nominal simultaneous scope over the returned grid separately for each query point. They do not provide joint coverage across subjects or predict an individual's event time.

docs.title: Re-running comparisons
docs.text: Install the intended R checkout in a shared R library. Put Rscript on PATH or set RLT_RSCRIPT to its executable path, then run the Python tests. Use R_LIBS_USER to select an existing shared user library when needed. R comparisons are skipped when Rscript is unavailable or RLT_SKIP_R_TESTS is set; an ordinary Python-only CI pass therefore does not establish cross-language agreement.

docs.title: RLT_cla
docs.text:
RLT_cla fits classification forests and returns class labels or probabilities through a sklearn-compatible interface. Ordinary integer or string label arrays use sorted observed classes. A pandas categorical response retains its declared levels and order, including unused levels and explicitly categorical numeric labels such as 0.25 and 0.75. classes_ determines probability-column order and tie breaking; predict returns labels in their original type.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_cla

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(100, 5))
y = rng.binomial(1, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-2 * X[:, 0])))

model = RLT_cla(n_estimators=500, random_state=42)
model.fit(X, y)                # string labels fine
prob = model.predict_proba(X)  # (n, n_classes)

docs.title: RLT_reg
docs.text:
RLT_reg fits regression forests with axis-aligned or linear-combination splits. Embedded forests can rank predictors for reinforcement and linear-combination splitting. The estimator follows the sklearn interface.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_reg

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(100, 5))
y = X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] + rng.normal(size=100)

model = RLT_reg(n_estimators=500, random_state=42)
model.fit(X, y)
pred = model.predict(X)

Supplied RNG objects advance. Repeat with the same data, effective parameters, and numerical environment.

docs.title: Variance settings
docs.text:
For all three estimators, fitting with var_mode adjusts the sampling settings after parameter defaults are resolved:

  • "matched" uses paired half-samples without replacement, setting resample_prob=0.5 and resample_replace=False. An odd tree count is reduced to the preceding even count; at least two trees are required.
  • "ij" and "jack" set resample_replace=True and keep the resolved resample_prob. These modes estimate prediction variance, not variable importance variance.

All active variance modes retain sampling counts and change importance="none" to "distribute". An explicitly selected "permute" or "distribute" method is retained. These modes supply their own sampling scheme and ignore a supplied resample_preset. Inspect model.params_ after fitting for the effective settings.

docs.title: Embedded-model controls
docs.text:
Embedded forests rank predictors within the current node. With linear_comb=1, reinforcement=True selects this ranking for split-variable selection. With linear_comb>1, regression and classification use embedded ranking in nodes with at least 3 * embed_nmin observations, even when reinforcement=False; smaller nodes use direct screening. Survival combination splits screen mtry candidates without an embedded forest. Setting an embed_* parameter alone does not enable either splitting mode.

The following controls are shared by the estimators. Here n is the total training sample size and p is the number of predictors. Proportions for embedded sampling and candidate selection refer to the current node and its available predictors.

Parameter Type Default Meaning embed_ntrees int 50 Number of trees in each embedded forest, with a minimum of 1. embed_mtry float 0.5 Candidates per embedded split: a proportion of available predictors below 1, or a count at least 1. The resulting count is truncated to an integer. Values are clamped to [0, p]. embed_nmin int 5 Embedded-tree node-size stopping threshold, with a minimum of 1. Nodes with at most this many observations stop; child nodes can be smaller. Also sets the 3 * embed_nmin switch described above. embed_nsplit int 3 Random cut points per candidate in the embedded forest; 0 considers all cut points. Values are clamped to be nonnegative. embed_resample_replace bool True Whether each embedded tree samples with replacement. embed_resample_prob float 0.9 Fraction of the current node's observations sampled for each embedded tree, clamped to [0, 0.99]. embed_mute float 0 Requested removal of low-ranked predictors from descendant candidate sets: a proportion below 1, or a count at least 1. Zero disables muting; protected predictors are retained, so fewer may be removed. Values are clamped to [0, p]. embed_protect int or None None Maximum number of top-ranked predictors added to the protected set for axis-aligned reinforcement or regression combinations, subject to embed_threshold. None uses ceil(log(n)), with the natural logarithm. Explicit values are clamped to [0, p]; a positive value is required for reinforcement or combination splits. Classification combinations instead protect their threshold-qualified candidate pool. embed_threshold float 0.25 Importance cutoff relative to the best embedded importance, clamped to [0, 1]. It controls entry into the protected set and also screens classification combination candidates in large nodes. It does not filter regression combination candidates.

docs.title: RLT_surv
docs.text:
RLT survival forest, a sklearn-compatible estimator porting the RLT R package's RLT(model = "survival") for right-censored time-to-event data.

RLT_surv grows a forest of survival trees and predicts individual survival functions, cumulative hazards, and optional cumulative-hazard covariances for simultaneous confidence bands.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_surv

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 200
X = rng.normal(size=(n, 5))
t_event = rng.exponential(1 / np.exp(X[:, 0]))
t_censor = rng.uniform(0, 3, size=n)

y = np.empty(n, dtype=[("event", "?"), ("time", float)])  # sksurv convention
y["event"] = t_event <= t_censor
y["time"] = np.minimum(t_event, t_censor)

model = RLT_surv(split_rule="logrank", random_state=42)
model.fit(X, y)
S = model.predict_survival_function(X)   # (n, T) survival curves
model.score(X, y)                        # fitted-data c-index, not validation

docs.title: Response format
docs.text:
y must be either

  • a structured array with fields event (0/1 or bool; 1 = event observed) and time (the scikit-survival convention), or
  • a (time, event) pair of arrays.

fit() validates the response and raises ValueError for NaN/Inf in time ("NA/Inf not permitted in y"), NaN in event ("NA not permitted in censor"), or event values outside {0, 1} ("censor must be 0 or 1"). Note that NaN in event can only arrive through a floating event array; a structured bool event field cannot hold NaN. Both tuple components and structured fields must be vectors; one-column inputs are accepted with a warning.

Parameter Type / values Default Description split_rule "logrank", "suplogrank", "coxgrad", or codes 1, 2, 3 "logrank" Splitting criterion for survival trees. Integral numeric codes such as 2.0 are also accepted. time_grid_size int 0 Fitting retains every unique failure time. Zero or a size at least as large as the full grid is accepted; smaller positive values are rejected. Use band_grid_size when predicting on a reduced grid. linear_comb_method "default", "coxph", "naive" or code 1 to 2 "default" Local Cox coefficients ("coxph", code 1, the default) or weighted survival score statistics ("naive", code 2). Integral doubles are accepted. Unknown names/out-of-range codes warn and reset to coxph; fractional and nonfinite codes are rejected. alpha float 0 Clamped to [0, 0.5] at fit, like R. categorical_features bool mask / int indices / None None See RLT_reg; same behavior for all three estimators.

linear_comb=k allows up to k variables in a split direction; some splits use fewer. All three survival split rules support observation weights. Weighted logrank and suplogrank account for weights in their split-score variance calculation. sample_weight must be finite and nonnegative with positive total mass, and does not change tree sampling. Individual zero weights are allowed, but a sampled outer or embedded tree with zero total weight raises an error.

var_mode="matched" uses paired half-samples without replacement. It enforces resample_prob=0.5 and resample_replace=False, reduces an odd tree count to the preceding even number, and requires at least two trees. The effective count is model.params_.ntrees. See RLT_reg for the shared variance-mode and observation-tracking settings.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Returns Description fit(X, y, sample_weight=None, var_prob=None, *, resample_preset=None) self Grow the forest with optional observation weights, variable-sampling probabilities and signed sampling counts. Observation weights do not replace the chosen split rule. predict(X, band_grid_size=0) (n, T) ndarray Default survival prediction: S(t \| x). predict_survival_function(X, band_grid_size=0) (n, T) ndarray Survival probabilities S(t \| x). predict_cumulative_hazard_function(X, band_grid_size=0) (n, T) ndarray Cumulative hazard H(t \| x). predict_risk(X) (n,) ndarray Risk score (cumulative hazard summed over the grid). predict_details(X, *, var_est=False, var_mode=None, keep_all=False, band_grid_size=0) dict Hazard increments, CHF, survival, exact timepoints, and optional CHF covariance and per-tree hazards. predict_all_trees(X, band_grid_size=0) (n, trees, times) ndarray Per-tree hazard increments. oob_details() dict OOB hazards on the full training grid, with counts and availability mask. tree_summary(tree=0) / print_tree(tree=0) dict Readable splits and terminal hazard vectors. predict_var(X, var_mode=None, band_grid_size=0) (S, cov) Survival curves plus per-subject CHF covariance of shape (n, T, T); requires a fitted variance mode or an explicit compatible prediction-time mode. importance_table() ImportanceTable Variable-importance summary (Variable / VI, plus SD / Z / Sig when fitted with importance != "none" and var_mode="matched"); same as rlt.importance(model). score(X, y) float Harrell's c-index (higher is better). forest_kernel(X1, X2=None, vs_train=False, oob=False) integer ndarray, or dict with oob=True Forest similarity kernel. get_one_tree(tree_id) dict Copied raw arrays and nested node-hazard vectors of tree tree_id (zero-based).

band_grid_size restricts returned predictions and covariance matrices to a reduced empirical-quantile grid. Hazard increments are accumulated on the full failure-time grid before selecting the requested times. Reducing the output grid therefore does not change the cumulative hazard or survival estimate at a retained time.

Ordinary forests return exp(-CHF) as survival. Linear combination forests return the mean of tree product-limit survival curves, which can differ from exp(-CHF). In both cases predict_var returns CHF covariance, not covariance of the returned survival estimate.

docs.title: Fitted attributes
docs.text: Attribute Shape Description forest_ dict The full fitted forest. timepoints_ (T,) Sorted unique failure-time grid. nfail_ int Number of failure times. oob_hazard_ (n, T) Out-of-bag hazard increments on the full training failure grid. oob_counts_ (n,) Number of eligible OOB predictions per row; use oob_details() to mask unavailable rows. oob_error_ float One minus concordance using the sum of OOB cumulative hazards over the full grid as risk, restricted to rows with OOB predictions. feature_importances_ (p,) Decrease in OOB concordance after perturbing each variable (when importance != "none"), rather than a decrease in the split statistic. var_vi_ (p,) Per-variable variance of the VI estimates (when importance != "none" and var_mode="matched"). obstrack_ (n, trees) Signed sampling-count matrix, with trees = params_.ntrees (when tracked). n_features_in_ int Number of predictors.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_surv, get_surv_band

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p = 200, 5
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
t_event = rng.exponential(1 / np.exp(X[:, 0]))
t_censor = rng.uniform(0, 3, size=n)

y = np.empty(n, dtype=[("event", "?"), ("time", float)])
y["event"] = t_event <= t_censor
y["time"] = np.minimum(t_event, t_censor)

# Variance-enabled forest and simultaneous bands
model = RLT_surv(n_estimators=1000, var_mode="matched",
                 resample_prob=0.5, resample_replace=False, random_state=0)
model.fit(X, y)

# Training rows illustrate returned arrays, not predictive validation.
prediction = model.predict_details(X[:2], var_est=True)
S, cov = prediction["Survival"], prediction["Cov"]
reference = np.exp(-prediction["CHF"])
band = get_surv_band(prediction, alpha=0.05, approach="smoothed")
band["lower"].shape, band["upper"].shape  # (2, T) each

The band uses reference and CHF covariance. Its nominal coverage is specified separately for each target over the saved time grid, with no joint guarantee across targets or coverage between grid points. It is not a prediction interval for an event time. See get_surv_band for the LC survival distinction.

For LC tree inspection, tree_summary() gives readable split directions. Raw SplitVar and SplitLoad arrays from get_one_tree() include every node. Internal nodes satisfy SplitVar[:, 0] >= 0; use that mask for both arrays when selecting internal-node coefficients.
