docs.title: RLT Classification Tutorial
docs.text: Use a classification forest to predict class labels and probabilities from numeric and categorical predictors. We simulate a binary response, fit on 80 observations, and evaluate predictions on 20 held-out observations.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install the current source as described in Get Started, then import it:

from rlt import RLT_cla

docs.title: Data Preparation
docs.text:
The first five predictors are numeric and the last five contain integer-coded categories. The probability of class 1 increases with the first numeric predictor; the other predictors have no effect on the simulated response.

import numpy as np

# (Optional) For reproducibility in this tutorial only.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

# ---- Generate a small synthetic dataset ----
trainn = 80
testn = 20
n = trainn + testn
p = 10

# Continuous + categorical predictors (last half as categorical)
X1 = rng.normal(size=(n, p // 2))
X2 = (rng.uniform(size=(n, p // 2)) * 10).astype(int)  # integers 0-9
X = np.hstack([X1, X2])

# Binary outcome via a simple logistic signal
def sigmoid(x):
    return np.exp(x) / (1 + np.exp(x))

prob = sigmoid(-0.5 + 2 * X[:, 0])  # signal in the first continuous feature
y = rng.binomial(1, p=prob)

# Train / test split
trainX, trainY = X[:trainn], y[:trainn]
testX, testY = X[trainn:], y[trainn:]

docs.title: Fit a classification model
docs.text:
Declare the last five columns in categorical_features to use categorical splits. The forest uses 200 trees and samples five candidate predictors at each node with mtry=p // 2. Setting nsplit=0 searches all available cutpoints for numeric candidates. The explicit random_state controls fitting randomness; rng above controls data generation. See Seeds & Reproducibility for details.

from rlt import RLT_cla

ntrees = 200
nmin = 5
mtry = p // 2
samplereplace = True
sampleprob = 0.80
rule = "best"
nsplit = 0 if rule == "best" else 3
importance = "permute"

fit = RLT_cla(
    n_estimators=ntrees,
    mtry=mtry,
    min_samples_leaf=nmin,
    resample_prob=sampleprob,
    resample_replace=samplereplace,
    nsplit=nsplit,
    importance=importance,
    categorical_features=range(p // 2, p),
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit.fit(trainX, trainY)

docs.title: Predict
docs.text:
# Predicted class labels (original label type: 0/1 here)
labels = fit.predict(testX)

# Class-membership probabilities, shape (n, n_classes)
proba = fit.predict_proba(testX)

# Decode the OOB class codes using the training label dictionary
oob_labels = fit.classes_[fit.oob_class_]

print("Probability columns:", fit.classes_)
print("Observed  Predicted  P(0)   P(1)")
for observed, predicted, row in zip(testY[:5], labels[:5], proba[:5]):
    print(f"{observed:8d}  {predicted:9d}  {row[0]:.3f}  {row[1]:.3f}")

Probability columns: [0 1]
Observed  Predicted  P(0)   P(1)
       0          0  0.772  0.228
       0          1  0.344  0.656
       0          0  0.882  0.118
       1          1  0.392  0.608
       0          0  0.809  0.191

predict() returns labels in their original type. Probability column j corresponds to fit.classes_[j], so the two columns here give probabilities of classes 0 and 1. Each row sums to one, and the predicted label has the largest probability. classes_ is the class order to use for both predict_proba() and oob_prob_. For an ordinary label array it contains sorted unique labels; for a pandas categorical response it preserves the declared category order, including unused categories.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
acc_oob = float(np.mean(oob_labels == trainY))
acc_test = float(np.mean(labels == testY))

# A compact summary
print(f"OOB accuracy:  {acc_oob:.4f}")
print(f"Test accuracy:  {acc_test:.4f}")

OOB accuracy:  0.8000
Test accuracy:  0.7500

Each OOB class prediction uses only trees that omitted that training observation. Test accuracy evaluates the separate held-out observations. Accuracy is the fraction of correctly classified observations, so larger values indicate better classification. With only 20 test observations, each additional correct classification changes test accuracy by 0.05.

docs.title: Inspect the fitted object
docs.text:
print(fit)

RLT_cla(categorical_features=range(5, 10), importance='permute', mtry=5,
        n_estimators=200, n_jobs=1, random_state=1, resample_prob=0.8)

Fitted attributes worth knowing:

fit.classes_          # class labels in probability-column order
fit.n_features_in_    # number of predictors
fit.oob_error_        # out-of-bag misclassification rate
fit.oob_class_        # (n,) OOB predicted classes (integer codes)
fit.oob_prob_         # (n, n_classes) OOB class probabilities
fit.feature_importances_  # (p,) variable importance

With the data above: fit.classes_ is array([0, 1]), fit.n_features_in_ is 10, and fit.oob_error_ is 0.2000.

String labels work too: RLT_cla stores classes_ and predict returns the original label type:

y_str = np.array(["neg", "pos"])[y]
fit2 = RLT_cla(n_estimators=200, random_state=1,
               categorical_features=range(p // 2, p))
fit2.fit(X, y_str)
fit2.classes_        # array(['neg', 'pos'], dtype='<U3')
fit2.predict(X[:3])  # e.g. array(['pos', 'neg', 'neg'], dtype='<U3')

docs.title: Prediction variance
docs.text:
Classification forests support variance estimation too, the equivalent of R's predict(fit, var.est = TRUE). Fit with var_mode (see the survival tutorial for the full variance story), then call predict_var() to get the class probabilities together with their variance:

fit_v = RLT_cla(
    n_estimators=500,
    var_mode="matched",
    categorical_features=range(p // 2, p),
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit_v.fit(trainX, trainY)

probs, variances = fit_v.predict_var(testX)

probs.shape      # (n, n_classes); same values as predict_proba
variances.shape  # (n, n_classes)

np.round(variances[:3], 5)

array([[0.00848, 0.00848],
       [0.01075, 0.01075],
       [0.00958, 0.00958]])

With two classes the two variance columns are identical (the second probability is one minus the first). Note that negative variance estimates are cleaned to NaN before returning; check with np.isnan(variances).any() and drop or inspect those cells rather than propagating them into downstream summaries. Variance estimation generally needs more trees than a prediction-only illustration. The 500 trees here demonstrate the calculation; this count does not establish its accuracy.

docs.title: Get Started with rlt
docs.text: Install rlt, fit a regression forest, and evaluate predictions on observations held out before fitting. The example also distinguishes an ordinary forest from reinforcement and linear-combination splits.

docs.title: Install the rlt package
docs.text:
These guides describe version 0.3.0 from the GitHub source. Use a shared user-wide or machine-wide Python installation, with Python 3.10 or later. The source build needs Armadillo, LAPACK, BLAS, OpenMP, and a C++17 compiler. On Debian/Ubuntu, install the shared system libraries with:

sudo apt-get install -y libarmadillo-dev liblapack-dev \
    libopenblas-dev libomp-dev g++

Install the build tools in your shared Python installation, then build the current source without an isolated build environment:

python -m pip install setuptools wheel pybind11
git clone https://github.com/teazrq/RLT-Python
cd RLT-Python
python -m pip install --no-build-isolation .

The commands above target Linux. See platform notes for Windows and macOS. For plotting the examples in the feature articles, install matplotlib in the same shared Python installation.

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
Run this from outside the cloned repository to check the installed package:

import rlt

print(rlt.__version__)
print(rlt.__file__)

The version should be 0.3.0. The path identifies which installation Python loaded. Different source revisions can share a version number; record git rev-parse HEAD in the checkout when you need to reproduce a source build.

docs.title: Fit and evaluate a regression forest
docs.text:
We will predict a continuous response from six numeric predictors. The response depends on the first two predictors plus independent noise. Reserve 40 rows for evaluation and use the other 160 to fit the forest:

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_reg

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 6))
y = X[:, 0] - X[:, 1] + rng.normal(size=200)

trainX, trainY = X[:160], y[:160]
testX, testY = X[160:], y[160:]

The default forest uses one variable per split. Here mtry=3 samples three candidate variables at each node, and nsplit=0 searches all available cutpoints for those candidates. Each tree makes 128 draws with replacement from the training set. We use 100 trees for this short example and fix random_state to control fitting randomness.

settings = dict(
    n_estimators=100, mtry=3, nsplit=0,
    resample_replace=True, resample_prob=0.8,
    random_state=1, n_jobs=1,
)
model = RLT_reg(**settings).fit(trainX, trainY)
pred = model.predict(testX)

print(f"OOB MSE: {model.oob_error_:.3f}")
print(f"Test MSE: {np.mean((pred - testY) ** 2):.3f}")
print("Observed  Predicted")
for observed, predicted in zip(testY[:5], pred[:5]):
    print(f"{observed:8.2f}  {predicted:9.2f}")

OOB MSE: 1.401
Test MSE: 1.847
Observed  Predicted
    1.47       0.78
    3.20       0.73
    0.50      -0.20
    2.96       2.88
   -0.29       0.25

The predictions estimate the mean response at each row's predictor values; individual responses also contain noise. Both errors are mean squared errors (MSEs), so smaller values indicate more accurate predictions. Each OOB prediction uses only trees that omitted that training observation. Test MSE evaluates the 40 separate observations reserved before fitting. These estimates can differ in a small sample; this example is not a performance benchmark.

docs.title: Try reinforcement or linear-combination splits
docs.text:
Reinforcement fits embedded forests within nodes to guide variable selection. Keep the data and outer forest settings fixed while requesting it:

reinforced = RLT_reg(reinforcement=True, **settings).fit(trainX, trainY)
reinforced_pred = reinforced.predict(testX)

We explicitly set the tree count in both fits because its default is 500 for an ordinary forest and 100 with reinforcement. This example demonstrates the control without establishing an accuracy advantage.

Linear-combination splits instead choose a direction formed from up to linear_comb predictors. They do not require reinforcement:

combined = RLT_reg(linear_comb=2, **settings).fit(trainX, trainY)
combined_pred = combined.predict(testX)

The linear-combination guide explains direction estimation. The embedded-model reference describes variable screening and its controls.

docs.title: Categorical predictors
docs.text:
Pandas is optional. In a pandas data frame, unordered Categorical columns automatically use categorical splits, preserving declared levels, including unused ones. Ordered categoricals and string columns use numerical ranks. For nominal labels with no meaningful order, use an unordered pandas Categorical column so splits can group levels rather than threshold their ranks. Prediction matches named columns and reuses the fitted label dictionary; unknown labels and missing values are rejected. Install pandas in your shared Python installation with python -m pip install pandas when using this optional input path.

Plain numeric arrays remain supported. Declare their nominal columns with categorical_features and supply non-negative integer level codes (0, 1, ..., k-1):

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_reg

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 100
X = np.hstack([
    rng.normal(size=(n, 2)),           # continuous columns 0-1
    rng.integers(0, 3, size=(n, 1)),   # 3-level categorical, column 2
    rng.integers(0, 2, size=(n, 1)),   # binary categorical, column 3
])
y = X[:, 0] + np.isin(X[:, 2], [1, 2]) + rng.normal(size=n)

# Integer indices of the categorical columns...
model = RLT_reg(n_estimators=100, categorical_features=[2, 3],
                random_state=0).fit(X, y)

# ...or an equivalent boolean mask of length p
model = RLT_reg(n_estimators=100,
                categorical_features=[False, False, True, True],
                random_state=0).fit(X, y)

model.ncat_  # array([1, 1, 3, 2]); 1 = continuous, k = k-level categorical

Rules to keep in mind:

  • Nominal columns in a plain numeric array must use non-negative integer codes 0..k-1; other values raise a ValueError.
  • A numeric prediction column for a fitted labeled predictor means zero-based training codes. Retain a pandas categorical dtype when supplying numeric labels such as 10, 2, and 1, so they are matched as labels rather than interpreted as codes.
  • A categorical column may have at most 53 levels (ValueError beyond that, matching the R package). Ordered and string rank encodings use numerical splits rather than categorical splits.
  • A numerical column with few unique values (up to 10) can trigger a UserWarning suggesting an explicit categorical declaration. It remains numerical unless declared otherwise.

See Model Workflows for category reordering and declared response-class levels.

docs.title: Platform notes
docs.text: The standard build configuration and CI target Linux with GCC and OpenMP. macOS and Windows builds require platform-specific compiler and linker configuration; the commands above are not a tested installation recipe for those platforms. Set n_jobs on the estimator to control forest parallelism.

docs.title: Randomness and reproducibility
docs.text:
Pass an integer random_state for a repeatable forest seed, separately from the NumPy generator used to simulate data:

from rlt import RLT_reg

model = RLT_reg(n_estimators=200, random_state=42)
model.fit(X, y)

The same integer seed, data, parameters, and numerical environment support repeatable fits. Cross-platform bitwise identity is not promised. With random_state=None, fitting draws from NumPy's global RNG, so np.random.seed(...) controls omitted forest seeds. See the Seeds & Reproducibility article for the full story, including how seeds interact with data simulation.

docs.title: RLT Regression Tutorial
docs.text: Use a regression forest to predict a continuous response from numeric and categorical predictors. We simulate a known signal, fit on 80 observations, and evaluate predictions on 20 held-out observations.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install the current source as described in Get Started, then import it:

from rlt import RLT_reg

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
The first five predictors are numeric and the last five contain integer-coded categories. The response combines predictors at indices 1 through 5, an additional effect for categories 1 and 2 of predictor 5, and independent Gaussian noise. Python column indices start at zero.

import numpy as np

# (Optional) For reproducibility in this tutorial only.
# Detailed notes on random seeds are in the Seed & Reproducibility article.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

# ---- Generate a small synthetic dataset ----
trainn = 80
testn = 20
n = trainn + testn
p = 10

# Continuous + categorical predictors (last half as categorical)
X1 = rng.normal(size=(n, p // 2))
X2 = (rng.uniform(size=(n, p // 2)) * 3).astype(int)  # integers 0, 1, 2

X = np.hstack([X1, X2])

# Continuous outcome with a simple signal + noise
y = (
    1
    + X[:, 1:6].sum(axis=1)
    + 2 * np.isin(X[:, p // 2], [1, 2])
    + rng.normal(size=n)
)

# Train / test split
trainX, trainY = X[:trainn], y[:trainn]
testX, testY = X[trainn:], y[trainn:]

docs.title: Fit
docs.text:
Declare the last five columns in categorical_features to use categorical splits. The forest uses 200 trees and samples five candidate predictors at each node with mtry=p // 2. Setting nsplit=0 searches all available cutpoints for numeric candidates. The explicit random_state controls fitting randomness; rng above controls data generation. See Seeds & Reproducibility for details.

from rlt import RLT_reg

ntrees = 200
nmin = 5
mtry = p // 2
samplereplace = True
sampleprob = 0.80
rule = "best"
nsplit = 0 if rule == "best" else 3  # 0 = consider all cut points
importance = "permute"

fit = RLT_reg(
    n_estimators=ntrees,
    mtry=mtry,
    min_samples_leaf=nmin,
    resample_prob=sampleprob,
    resample_replace=samplereplace,
    nsplit=nsplit,
    importance=importance,
    categorical_features=range(p // 2, p),
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit.fit(trainX, trainY)

docs.title: Predict
docs.text:
pred = fit.predict(testX)

# OOB (out-of-bag) predictions and error are computed during the fit
oob_pred = fit.oob_prediction_
test_pred = pred

print("Observed  Predicted")
for observed, predicted in zip(testY[:5], test_pred[:5]):
    print(f"{observed:8.3f}  {predicted:9.3f}")

Observed  Predicted
   4.242      3.456
   4.893      4.464
  -1.416      1.433
   6.339      4.525
   5.782      5.120

predict() returns one numeric prediction per held-out row, estimating the conditional mean response at those predictor values. Individual responses also contain noise, so predictions need not match them exactly.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
mse_oob = float(np.mean((oob_pred - trainY) ** 2))
mse_test = float(np.mean((test_pred - testY) ** 2))

# A compact summary
print(f"OOB MSE:  {mse_oob:.4f}")
print(f"Test MSE:  {mse_test:.4f}")

OOB MSE:  2.4167
Test MSE:  4.6647

Each OOB prediction uses only trees that omitted that training observation. The test MSE evaluates the separate held-out observations. Both are mean squared errors, with smaller values indicating more accurate predictions. Their difference reflects the different evaluation samples and trees used; the test estimate is noisy with only 20 observations.

docs.title: Inspect
docs.text:
print(fit)

RLT_reg(categorical_features=range(5, 10), importance='permute', mtry=5,
        n_estimators=200, n_jobs=1, random_state=1, resample_prob=0.8)

Fitted attributes worth knowing:

fit.n_features_in_          # number of predictors
fit.oob_error_              # out-of-bag MSE (also = MSE of oob_prediction_)
fit.oob_prediction_         # (n,) OOB training predictions
fit.feature_importances_    # (p,) variable importance
fit.get_one_tree(0)         # raw arrays of tree 0; see Single Tree article

To assess which predictors the forest relies on, continue to Variable Importance.

docs.title: RLT Survival Analysis Tutorial
docs.text:
This vignette introduces survival analysis with rlt (Reinforcement Learning Trees). RLT survival forests estimate conditional survival probabilities and cumulative hazards, and return hazard increments on an observed failure-time grid. Key features include:

  • Three split rules: logrank (default), suplogrank, and coxgrad.
  • Linear combination (LC) splits: combine multiple variables into a single split direction.
  • Variance estimation: matched-sample U-statistic, infinitesimal jackknife (IJ), and jackknife.
  • Confidence bands: get_surv_band() provides naive or smoothed simultaneous bands for survival curves.
  • Tree inspection: get_one_tree() inspects individual tree structures.

The examples below use small simulated datasets so that all code runs quickly.

docs.title: Simulated data
docs.text:
We simulate data from a proportional hazards model with exponential event times and independent censoring. The first two predictors carry signal; the rest are noise.

import numpy as np
from rlt import RLT_surv

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 200
p = 5
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))

beta = np.array([0.8, 0.5, 0, 0, 0])
hazard = np.exp(X @ beta)
surv_time = rng.exponential(1.0 / hazard)
censor_time = rng.uniform(0, 3, size=n)

time = np.minimum(surv_time, censor_time)
event = (surv_time <= censor_time).astype(int)

np.bincount(event)  # 0 = censored, 1 = observed event

Responses follow the scikit-survival convention: a structured array with event and time fields (1 = event observed, 0 = censored):

y = np.empty(n, dtype=[("event", "?"), ("time", "<f8")])
y["event"] = event.astype(bool)
y["time"] = time

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
Fit a survival forest with RLT_surv. By default split_rule="logrank".

fit = RLT_surv(
    n_estimators=100,
    min_samples_leaf=5,
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=42,
)
fit.fit(X, y)

Predict at selected predictor values to obtain survival curves and cumulative hazards. Here five training rows illustrate the returned arrays. These predictions use all trees and do not evaluate out-of-sample performance:

S = fit.predict_survival_function(X[:5])        # S(t), shape (5, T)
chf = fit.predict_cumulative_hazard_function(X[:5])  # H(t), shape (5, T)

# T is the number of unique failure times
fit.timepoints_.shape

Each component is an n x T matrix, where T is the number of unique failure times (fit.timepoints_). On this full grid, the hazard increment h(t) can be recovered from the cumulative hazard:

hazard = np.diff(chf, prepend=0.0, axis=1)  # h(t) at each failure time

Plot the predicted survival curve for the first subject:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4.3))
plt.step(fit.timepoints_, S[0], where="post")
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Survival Probability")
plt.title("Predicted Survival Curve (Subject 1)")
plt.ylim(0, 1)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Select a figure to view it at full size.

Each downward step lowers the estimated probability of survival beyond that time; flat segments indicate no change between failure times. This is a conditional curve at one subject's predictor values. For this ordinary forest, S equals np.exp(-chf).

docs.title: Response validation
docs.text:
fit() checks survival times and event indicators before growing the forest. Missing or invalid values raise a ValueError:

# NaN/Inf in time
y_bad_time = y.copy()
y_bad_time["time"][0] = np.nan

# A floating event array can contain NaN; a structured bool field cannot.
event_nan = np.concatenate([[np.nan], np.ones(n - 1)])

# Event values must be 0 or 1.
event_bad = np.full(n, 2.0)

for y_try in (y_bad_time, (y["time"], event_nan), (y["time"], event_bad)):
    try:
        RLT_surv(n_estimators=20, n_jobs=1, random_state=0).fit(X, y_try)
    except ValueError as err:
        print("ValueError:", err)

ValueError: NA/Inf not permitted in y
ValueError: NA not permitted in censor
ValueError: censor must be 0 or 1

Check invalid outcomes against the source records and the study's event and censoring definitions. Handling missing outcomes requires an analysis decision; arbitrary imputation or recoding changes the survival data.

docs.title: Split rules
docs.text:
rlt provides three splitting criteria for survival trees:

Rule How it scores a split logrank Standard log-rank test statistic (default) suplogrank Maximum of the standardized log-rank process over time coxgrad Gradient of Cox partial likelihood

Fit the three rules on the same data and compare out-of-bag error estimates. The error is 1 - C, using a risk score that sums the OOB cumulative hazards over the full failure-time grid. Lower values are better; this sum is neither the final cumulative hazard nor a time integral. Each observation's OOB predictions use trees fitted without that observation. Concordance is undefined without comparable event-time pairs.

fit_lr = RLT_surv(n_estimators=100, split_rule="logrank",
                  n_jobs=1, random_state=42)
fit_slr = RLT_surv(n_estimators=100, split_rule="suplogrank",
                   n_jobs=1, random_state=42)
fit_cg = RLT_surv(n_estimators=100, split_rule="coxgrad",
                  n_jobs=1, random_state=42)

fit_lr.fit(X, y); fit_slr.fit(X, y); fit_cg.fit(X, y)

print(f"logrank:     {fit_lr.oob_error_:.5f}")
print(f"suplogrank:  {fit_slr.oob_error_:.5f}")
print(f"coxgrad:     {fit_cg.oob_error_:.5f}")

logrank:     0.34945
suplogrank:  0.35366
coxgrad:     0.40004

These values describe this simulated dataset and do not establish a general ranking of the split rules. logrank is the default.

docs.title: Observation weights
docs.text:
Observation weights are passed via the sample_weight argument of fit. All three survival split rules use them; weighted logrank and suplogrank include weights in their split-score variance calculation. Weights must be finite and nonnegative with positive total mass. They do not change how observations are sampled for each tree. The arbitrary positive weights below illustrate the syntax and have no scientific interpretation in this simulation. Individual zero weights are allowed, but every sampled outer or embedded tree must have positive total weight; a zero-weight sampled tree raises an error.

w = rng.uniform(size=n)
fit_w = RLT_surv(n_estimators=100, split_rule="coxgrad",
                 n_jobs=1, random_state=1)
fit_w.fit(X, y, sample_weight=w)

docs.title: Linear combination splits
docs.text:
When linear_comb > 1, a split can combine up to linear_comb variables in one direction. For survival forests, the available methods are:

  • "coxph" (default): coefficients from a local Cox model fit.
  • "naive": direction based on weighted survival score statistics.
fit_lc = RLT_surv(
    n_estimators=100,
    split_rule="logrank",
    linear_comb=3,
    linear_comb_method="coxph",
    n_jobs=1,
    random_state=1,
)
fit_lc.fit(X, y)

Predictions from LC forests have the same structure as standard forests. Their survival estimate is the mean of tree product-limit curves, which can differ from exp(-CHF):

S_lc = fit_lc.predict_survival_function(X[:5])
S_lc.shape  # (5, T)

docs.title: Variable importance
docs.text:
Set importance="permute" to compute the decrease in OOB concordance after permuting a variable. Larger positive values indicate greater contribution to risk ordering. This measure differs from the statistic used to select a split. Outcomes with no comparable pairs cannot supply a defined importance contribution.

fit_imp = RLT_surv(n_estimators=100, importance="permute",
                   n_jobs=1, random_state=1)
fit_imp.fit(X, y)

np.round(fit_imp.feature_importances_, 3)

array([ 0.05 ,  0.036, -0.004, -0.003,  0.004])

The two signal variables have the largest importance estimates in this run. Small negative values can occur when permutation happens to improve OOB concordance; they do not imply a protective effect.

docs.title: Variance estimation and confidence bands
docs.text:
rlt supports three variance estimation strategies for survival predictions:

  • "matched": matched-sample U-statistic decomposition using paired half-samples without replacement and an even number of trees. See Xu, Zhu, and Shao (2024) for the variance estimation framework.
  • "ij": infinitesimal jackknife.
  • "jack": jackknife-after-bootstrap variance.

Enable variance estimation during fitting via var_mode, then save the prediction with its CHF covariance and time grid. Here 1,000 trees form 500 matched pairs. Matched mode enforces the resampling settings shown below and reduces an odd tree count to the preceding even count; it requires at least two trees.

fit_var = RLT_surv(n_estimators=1000, var_mode="matched",
                   resample_prob=0.5, resample_replace=False,
                   n_jobs=1, random_state=42)
fit_var.fit(X, y)

# Training rows illustrate the prediction format, not validation.
pred_var = fit_var.predict_details(X[:3], var_est=True)
Sv, cov = pred_var["Survival"], pred_var["Cov"]

# cov is an (n, T, T) array: covariance of the cumulative hazard over time
print(Sv.shape, cov.shape)  # (3, 131) (3, 131, 131)

predict_var() also returns (Sv, cov) when the full prediction dictionary is not needed. Variance estimation generally needs more trees than the small fitting examples above; 1,000 trees is an illustration, not a coverage guarantee.

docs.title: Confidence bands with get_surv_band()
docs.text:
The cumulative-hazard covariance and Gaussian simulation framework for survival bands is developed in Formentini, Liang, and Zhu (2022). See the get_surv_band reference for the current smoothing and covariance handling.

With alpha=0.05, get_surv_band() constructs a nominal 95% simultaneous band for each target's conditional survival curve over the returned time grid. This is neither joint coverage across targets nor continuous-time coverage between grid points, and it is not a prediction interval for an individual's event time.

The reference curve is np.exp(-pred_var["CHF"]). It equals returned survival for an ordinary forest. LC forests instead return the mean of tree product-limit curves; this CHF-based band does not directly estimate variation in that different estimator. Two approaches are available:

  • "naive": uses the full covariance matrix with a Monte Carlo critical value.
  • "smoothed": uses a smoothed low-rank covariance approximation with a residual correction to form marginal standardizing scales.

Both approaches simulate from the original supplied CHF covariance.

from rlt import get_surv_band

# Naive band for the first row in the saved prediction
band_naive = get_surv_band(pred_var, i=1, alpha=0.05,
                           approach="naive", nsim=5000)

# Smoothed band
band_smooth = get_surv_band(pred_var, i=1, alpha=0.05,
                            approach="smoothed", nsim=5000, k_rank=10)

Reuse the saved dictionary to compare band settings without recomputing forest predictions. Plot the CHF-based reference curve with the naive band, retaining the raw limits and restricting only the displayed axis:

t = band_naive["timepoints"]
S1 = np.exp(-pred_var["CHF"][0])

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4.3))
plt.step(t, S1, where="post", color="black", label="Estimate")
plt.step(t, band_naive["lower"][0], where="post", color="blue",
         linestyle="--", label="95% Band")
plt.step(t, band_naive["upper"][0], where="post", color="blue",
         linestyle="--")
plt.xlabel("Time"); plt.ylabel("Survival")
plt.title("Survival Curve with 95% Confidence Band")
plt.ylim(0, 1)
plt.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The band describes uncertainty about the conditional curve at these predictor values. This training-row illustration does not assess its coverage or predictive performance.

You can also request all subjects at once with i=0 (the default).

docs.title: Reducing the time grid for bands
docs.text:
For large datasets, the full set of failure times can make covariance matrices unwieldy. Use band_grid_size in predict_var() (or pass it to get_surv_band() with a fitted model and query covariates) to evaluate variance on a reduced quantile-based grid. A saved prediction already fixes its grid:

S3, cov3 = fit_var.predict_var(X[:3], band_grid_size=50)
S3.shape  # (3, 50), at most 50 time points

Selected quantiles can coincide, so the requested size is a maximum. Cumulative hazards still include increments at all earlier failure times. Bands on a reduced grid describe the selected times and do not establish coverage between omitted times.

docs.title: Inspecting individual trees
docs.text:
Use get_one_tree() to inspect the structure of any tree in the fitted forest. It returns the raw arrays of the tree (0-indexed):

tree = fit.get_one_tree(0)
tree.keys()

dict_keys(['SplitVar', 'SplitValue', 'LeftNode', 'RightNode', 'NodeWeight', 'NodeHaz'])

n_nodes = len(tree["SplitVar"])
n_splits = int((tree["SplitVar"] >= 0).sum())
print(f"{n_nodes} nodes, {n_splits} splits")

121 nodes, 60 splits

A node i is internal when SplitVar[i] >= 0: the split sends points with X[SplitVar[i]] <= SplitValue[i] to LeftNode[i] and the rest to RightNode[i]. Terminal nodes have SplitVar[i] == -1.

For LC forests, tree_summary() shows each split direction with its coefficients. Preview the first few nodes:

lc_summary = fit_lc.tree_summary(0)
for node in lc_summary["Node"][:5]:
    print(node, lc_summary["Split"][node], lc_summary["Value"][node])

Raw LC SplitVar and SplitLoad arrays have one row for every node, including terminal nodes. Apply the same internal-node mask to both:

lc_tree = fit_lc.get_one_tree(0)
lc_variables = np.asarray(lc_tree["SplitVar"])
lc_loadings = np.asarray(lc_tree["SplitLoad"])
internal = lc_variables[:, 0] >= 0
internal_variables = lc_variables[internal]
internal_loadings = lc_loadings[internal]
print(lc_loadings.shape, internal_loadings.shape)

(97, 3) (48, 3)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Fit a survival forest with RLT_surv().fit(X, y).
  • Predict with predict_survival_function() / predict_cumulative_hazard_function() to obtain S(t) and H(t).
  • Choose split_rule among "logrank", "suplogrank", and "coxgrad".
  • Use sample_weight for weighted fitting with any of the three split rules.
  • Allow up to k variables per LC split with linear_comb=k, linear_comb_method="coxph".
  • Request variable importance with importance="permute" and inspect via feature_importances_.
  • Estimate prediction variance with var_mode="matched" / "ij" / "jack", then call predict_var().
  • Build confidence bands from a saved prediction with get_surv_band(prediction, approach="naive" or "smoothed").
  • Inspect readable trees with tree_summary(i) or raw arrays with get_one_tree(i).
